paragraph: The necklace splitting problem, first introduced by Bhatt and Leiserson [ 6], is a classic 28 combinatorial fair division problem. In this work, we extend it to a dynamic setting, enabling 29 applications such as data-informed fair hash maps and improved load-balancing among 30 multiple servers.

Soon after the necklace splitting problem was originally introduced [ 6], Goldberg and West [ 9] 88 proved that a solution always exists if k= 2. Alon and West [ 3] gave a simpler proof using 89 the Borsuk–Ulam theorem [ 7], and Alon [ 1] generalized the results to k>2. Finally, Alon 90 and Graur [ 2] discovered an efficient approximation algorithm for finding a solution with few 91 cuts. Alon and Graur [ 2] also consider an online variation of the problem. They derive lower 92 and upper bounds on the number of cuts needed when k= 2based on the value of n. They 93 also generalize some of these results to the k>2case. 94 In addition to necklace splitting, other fair division problems can be extended to dynamic 95 settings. Kash et al. In this section, we discuss several key applications of the dynamic necklace splitting problem.

In addition to ensuring fairness, such data-informed hash maps can even be faster than 105 traditional hash maps [ 14,17]. Shahbazi et al. [ 19] use the static necklace splitting problem 106 to design hash maps that satisfy group fairness. However, making dynamic updates to these 107 hash maps is infeasible without a dynamic solution to the necklace splitting problem. 108 For a concrete application, consider the use of fair hash maps to maintain user information 109 on a social network. Whenever new users join the network, their data needs to be efficiently 110 added to the hash map, and when users leave, their data needs to be efficiently removed. 111 As users’ attributes change, their data needs to be efficiently updated (corresponding to 112 relocation of beads in a necklace). 113 Another concrete application involves table joins in data lakes. Consider an organization 114 seeking to share its data with third parties. The data is stored in a data lake and includes 115 sensitive information as primary keys for certain tables. To protect user privacy, the data 116 needs to be hashed, which introduces the risk of hash collision. A fair hashing scheme 117 must be used to ensure any resulting errors when joining on the hashed columns do not 118 disproportionately impact a specific demographic group [ 19]. For this system to be efficient, 119 it needs to be easy to update the hashes as the data changes.

Consider the problem of load-balancing among multiple servers, where tasks need to be 122 completed in a specific order. Each agent corresponds to a server, and each bead color 123 corresponds to a different type of task. We want to spread the load across the servers evenly, 124 but we also want to minimize communication costs [ 12]. This necessitates having as few cuts 125 as possible. 126 If the order of tasks needs to be modified, new tasks need to be added, or existing tasks 127 need to be canceled, we would want to be able to update the computation plan without 128 recreating it from scratch. As a special case, if computation has already begun, we can 129 still perform dynamic updates that don’t affect the already-completed tasks using dynamic 130 necklace splitting.

Another key application is ensuring minority representation in bucketization. For example, 133 when partitioning data for machine learning tasks, it is crucial that the training data is 134 accurately represented by the test data for reliable results [ 18]. Intentionally designing the 135 bucketization process to maintain fairness helps prevent downstream fairness issues [ 15,16]. 136 Here, each agent represents a bucket, and the color of each bead represents the grouping 137 attribute. If the “red” data is more sparse than the “blue” data, it is important that the 138 relative proportions are preserved to have accurate results. 139

paragraph: In the first case, there is a cut to the left of the red bead and to the right of the blue 442 bead (or it is at the end of the necklace). This is the simplest case – we swap the beads and 443 let the agents retain ownership of their original beads. No cuts need to be adjusted. 444 In the second case, there is a cut on the left, but not the right. We swap the beads and do 445 not adjust any cuts. A2takes possession of the left interval, and A1takes possession of the 446 right interval. As part of the right interval, A1gains at least one unneeded extra bead (the 447 green one). Each extra bead lacks a cut to its left, so they must be the first of their colors. 448 Thus, the original beads of A1are somewhere to the right in the necklace. Furthermore, 449 since each of the original beads is not the first of its color, they each start their own intervals. 450 A2takes ownership of each of these intervals and repeats the process with each of them if 451 they have multiple beads, continuing to attempt to re-satisfy the fairness constraint. Since 452 the necklace has exactly n−1pairs of adjacent beads without a cut, this results in at most 453 nownership exchanges throughout the procedure. 454 In the third case, there is no cut on the left. We swap the beads and move the cut left 455 by one bead (to ensure that the set of cuts maintains the structure of one generated by the 456 offline algorithm). A1andA2retain the left and right intervals, respectively. Similarly to 457 the second case, to maintain the fairness constraint, at most n−1intervals will have to be 458 exchanged between the two agents. 459 We will henceforth refer to this procedure as DenseSwap . The two-dimensional array 460 allows us to perform each ownership exchange in constant time, giving a running time of 461 O(n)forDenseSwap . 462 ▶Theorem 15.
